terms.simpleExplanation: It's the standard technique used to raise a satellite from a low parking orbit up to a higher operational orbit like geostationary orbit.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Orbital Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: A deliberate change to a spacecraft's orbit, typically executed by firing thrusters to change its velocity.
terms.simpleExplanation: Every orbit adjustment, from station-keeping to an interplanetary transfer, is built from combinations of these velocity-changing burns.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Orbital Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The total change in velocity a spacecraft's propulsion system must be able to provide to complete its planned maneuvers.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the single most important number in mission planning — it directly determines how much propellant a spacecraft must carry.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Avionics
terms.simpleDefinition: The primary computer system that automates navigation, flight planning, and performance calculations in a modern aircraft.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the central 'brain' pilots interact with to program a route, and it feeds guidance commands to the autopilot.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Avionics
terms.simpleDefinition: A satellite-based navigation system that determines a receiver's precise position by measuring signal travel time from multiple satellites.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the primary means of precise aircraft navigation today, though inertial navigation remains valuable as a backup that doesn't depend on external signals.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Avionics
terms.simpleDefinition: A system that automatically controls an aircraft's flight path, holding a heading, altitude, or programmed route without constant pilot input.
terms.simpleExplanation: It significantly reduces pilot workload on long flights, though a human pilot remains responsible for monitoring and taking over when needed.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Avionics
terms.simpleDefinition: An aircraft cockpit design using electronic flight displays instead of traditional analog dial instruments.
terms.simpleExplanation: It consolidates dozens of individual gauges into a few configurable screens, reducing clutter and pilot workload.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Avionics
terms.simpleDefinition: A system that computes key flight parameters like airspeed, altitude, and Mach number from pressure and temperature sensor inputs.
terms.simpleExplanation: Nearly every other avionics and flight-control system on the aircraft depends on the accurate data it provides.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Flight Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: An aircraft's initial tendency to return toward its original equilibrium after being disturbed.
terms.simpleExplanation: A statically stable aircraft naturally noses back down after a gust pitches it up, without any pilot input.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Flight Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: How an aircraft's motion actually behaves over time following a disturbance — whether oscillations grow, shrink, or stay steady.
terms.simpleExplanation: An aircraft can be statically stable yet dynamically unstable if its corrective response overshoots and oscillates with increasing amplitude.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Flight Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: An aircraft's stability in pitch — its tendency to resist nose-up or nose-down disturbances around its lateral axis.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's primarily governed by the relationship between the center of gravity and the aircraft's aerodynamic center.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Flight Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: An aircraft's stability in yaw — its tendency to point back into the relative wind after a sideways disturbance.
terms.simpleExplanation: The vertical tail fin is the primary component providing this restoring tendency, much like the feathers on an arrow.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Flight Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The study of how an aircraft's speed, range, climb rate, and fuel efficiency depend on its design and the atmospheric conditions it flies in.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's used to determine practical operating limits like maximum range, service ceiling, and takeoff distance for a given aircraft.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Flight Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The maximum altitude at which an aircraft can still maintain a minimal specified rate of climb.
terms.simpleExplanation: Beyond this altitude the air is too thin for the aircraft to climb further at a meaningful rate, even at full power.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Flight Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The maximum distance an aircraft can fly on a given amount of fuel.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's a critical performance metric derived from the aircraft's fuel efficiency, weight, and aerodynamic characteristics using the Breguet range equation.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate aerospace engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: A circuit where components are connected end-to-end so the same current flows through each one.
terms.simpleExplanation: If one component in a series circuit fails open, the entire circuit stops conducting — like old-style Christmas lights.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: A circuit where components are connected across the same two nodes, so they all share the same voltage.
terms.simpleExplanation: Each branch can be analyzed independently, and if one branch fails, current can still flow through the others.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: A simple circuit of series resistors that splits an input voltage into a smaller, predictable output voltage.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's one of the most common building blocks in electronics, used anywhere a lower reference voltage is needed from a higher supply.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: A simple circuit of parallel resistors that splits an input current into predictable fractions through each branch.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the parallel-circuit counterpart to the voltage divider, useful whenever current needs to be shared between components.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: The technique of converting a voltage source with a series resistor into an equivalent current source with a parallel resistor, or vice versa.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's a handy simplification tool that can make an otherwise complex circuit much easier to analyze.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: A systematic circuit analysis technique that solves for the voltage at each node using Kirchhoff's current law.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's one of the two standard systematic methods (with mesh analysis) for solving circuits with many components.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: A systematic circuit analysis technique that solves for the current in each independent loop using Kirchhoff's voltage law.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's especially convenient for planar circuits with many series-connected loops.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: The opposition a capacitor or inductor presents to alternating current, which depends on the signal's frequency.
terms.simpleExplanation: Unlike resistance, it doesn't dissipate energy as heat — it stores and releases it, which is why it's treated separately in AC analysis.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: The overall ease with which an AC circuit allows current to flow, the reciprocal of impedance.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's especially convenient for analyzing parallel AC circuits, the same way conductance simplifies parallel DC circuits.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: The principle that maximum power is delivered to a load when the load's resistance equals the source's internal (Thevenin) resistance.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's why audio equipment and antennas are designed to be 'impedance matched' to whatever they're connected to.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: The condition in a series RLC circuit where inductive and capacitive reactance cancel, minimizing total impedance.
terms.simpleExplanation: At this frequency the circuit draws maximum current from the source, which is the basis for tuning circuits like radio receivers.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: The condition in a parallel RLC circuit where inductive and capacitive reactance cancel, maximizing total impedance.
terms.simpleExplanation: At this frequency the circuit draws minimum current from the source, the opposite behavior of series resonance.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: A dimensionless measure of how sharply 'tuned' a resonant circuit is, relating stored energy to energy dissipated per cycle.
terms.simpleExplanation: A higher quality factor means a sharper, more selective resonance peak, which is desirable in radio tuning circuits.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: The voltage measured between any two of the three lines in a three-phase power system.
terms.simpleExplanation: In a star-connected system, it's larger than the phase voltage by a factor of the square root of three.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Circuit Theory
terms.simpleDefinition: The voltage measured between one line and the neutral point in a three-phase power system.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the voltage each individual load in a balanced three-phase system actually experiences.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A graphical representation of a control system showing its components as blocks connected by signal-flow arrows.
terms.simpleExplanation: It lets an engineer visualize and algebraically manipulate how signals move through a complex control system.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A graphical representation of the relationships between variables in a system of linear equations, used as an alternative to block diagrams.
terms.simpleExplanation: Mason's gain formula can be applied directly to it to find an overall transfer function without step-by-step block diagram reduction.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: How a control system's output changes over time in reaction to a specific input, like a step or impulse.
terms.simpleExplanation: Engineers use it to judge whether a system responds quickly, smoothly, and accurately enough for its application.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: The difference between a control system's desired output and actual output after all transients have settled.
terms.simpleExplanation: A well-designed feedback system aims to drive this error toward zero for a given standard input.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A dimensionless parameter describing how oscillations in a system decay after a disturbance.
terms.simpleExplanation: A higher damping ratio means the system settles to steady-state more smoothly with less overshoot, at the cost of a slower response.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: The frequency at which a system would oscillate if there were no damping at all.
terms.simpleExplanation: Combined with the damping ratio, it fully characterizes how a standard second-order control system responds over time.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A measure of how much a system's gain can increase before it becomes unstable.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's read directly off a Bode plot and gives engineers a safety margin to design against for stable operation.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A measure of how much additional phase lag a system can tolerate at its gain crossover frequency before becoming unstable.
terms.simpleExplanation: Along with gain margin, it's a standard way engineers quantify how close a control system is to instability.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A graphical method for determining a closed-loop system's stability by examining how its open-loop frequency response encircles a critical point.
terms.simpleExplanation: It can assess stability directly from frequency-response data without needing to explicitly solve for the system's poles.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: An algebraic method for determining how many roots of a system's characteristic equation lie in the unstable region, without solving for the roots directly.
terms.simpleExplanation: It gives a quick yes/no stability answer directly from the coefficients of a system's characteristic equation.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A control action that produces an output correction directly proportional to the current error.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the simplest of the three PID actions, but alone it typically leaves some steady-state error uncorrected.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A control action that accumulates past error over time to drive steady-state error to zero.
terms.simpleExplanation: It eliminates the offset a pure proportional controller leaves behind, at the cost of potentially slower or more oscillatory response.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Control Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A control action that responds to the rate of change of the error, helping to dampen oscillations and anticipate future error.
terms.simpleExplanation: It adds a predictive, damping effect to a controller, improving stability and reducing overshoot.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: The rotating part of an electrical machine, such as a motor or generator.
terms.simpleExplanation: Its interaction with the stationary stator's magnetic field is what produces mechanical rotation or electrical generation.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: The stationary outer part of an electrical machine that houses the field windings or permanent magnets.
terms.simpleExplanation: It works together with the rotor to establish the magnetic fields that make the machine function.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: A rotating electrical switch in a DC machine that reverses current direction in the armature windings at the right moment.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's what allows a DC motor to keep spinning in one direction, or a DC generator to output a steady unidirectional voltage.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: A rotating electrical contact used to transfer current to or from a rotating part of a machine, without reversing its direction like a commutator.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's used in AC machines like alternators and wound-rotor induction motors, where current doesn't need switching.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: The winding in an electrical machine that produces the magnetic field the machine operates on.
terms.simpleExplanation: Its strength directly determines the machine's magnetic flux, and therefore the torque or voltage the machine produces.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: The winding in an electrical machine where the working voltage is induced (in a generator) or that produces torque (in a motor).
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the winding that actually does the machine's electromechanical work, as distinct from the field winding that sets up the magnetic field.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: A magnetic field whose direction continuously rotates in space, produced by properly-phased AC currents in stationary windings.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the key phenomenon that lets an AC induction motor spin without any electrical connection to its rotor.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: The fixed speed at which an AC machine's rotating magnetic field turns, determined by supply frequency and the number of poles.
terms.simpleExplanation: A synchronous motor locks exactly to this speed, while an induction motor always runs slightly slower than it.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: A curve showing how much torque a motor produces at each operating speed.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's used to match a motor to a mechanical load — a load's own torque-speed requirement must fall within what the motor can deliver.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electrical Machines
terms.simpleDefinition: The percentage change in a generator's terminal voltage from no-load to full-load conditions.
terms.simpleExplanation: A lower value means the generator holds its voltage steadier as load changes, which is generally more desirable.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A simplified schematic representing a three-phase power system using a single line, rather than drawing all three phases separately.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the standard way power engineers document and communicate the layout of a power network without unnecessary visual clutter.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: The overhead or underground conductors that carry electrical power over long distances from a generating station to substations.
terms.simpleExplanation: Its electrical characteristics — resistance, inductance, and capacitance — all affect how efficiently power can travel along it.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A facility that transforms voltage levels and switches connections within a power transmission and distribution network.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the critical link where high transmission voltages are stepped down for safer, more usable distribution voltages.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: The process of predicting future electricity demand to plan generation and transmission capacity.
terms.simpleExplanation: Accurate forecasts are essential for utilities to ensure enough generation is available without wastefully overbuilding capacity.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A power system's ability to remain in a stable operating state, or return to one, after being subjected to a disturbance.
terms.simpleExplanation: Losing it can trigger a cascading blackout, which is why it's one of the most heavily studied aspects of power system engineering.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: Techniques used to supply or absorb reactive power locally in a power network to improve voltage stability and efficiency.
terms.simpleExplanation: It reduces transmission losses and helps keep voltage levels within acceptable limits across the network.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: The process of allocating power output among multiple generating units to meet demand at the lowest total operating cost.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's a core optimization problem utilities solve continuously to run their generation fleet as economically as possible.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A power system fault, like a three-phase short circuit, where all three phases are affected equally.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the most severe type of fault electrically, even though it's statistically less common than unbalanced faults.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A power system fault that affects the three phases unequally, such as a single line-to-ground fault.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the most common type of fault in real power systems and requires more complex analysis techniques than a symmetrical fault.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: Silicon Controlled Rectifier — a four-layer semiconductor device that acts as a controllable switch, conducting only after being triggered.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's a common type of thyristor used to control power flow in applications ranging from motor drives to light dimmers.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A bidirectional semiconductor switch capable of conducting current in either direction once triggered.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's commonly used in household light dimmers and AC motor speed controllers because it can switch both halves of an AC waveform.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A protective circuit, typically a resistor-capacitor network, placed across a power switching device to limit voltage spikes and stress.
terms.simpleExplanation: It protects sensitive power semiconductors from the voltage transients that occur every time they switch on or off.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A DC-DC converter that steps down an input voltage to a lower, regulated output voltage.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's one of the most common power converter topologies, used in nearly every device that needs a lower voltage than its battery or supply provides.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A DC-DC converter that steps up an input voltage to a higher, regulated output voltage.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's used whenever a circuit needs a higher voltage than its power source directly provides, such as in some battery-powered devices.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A DC-DC converter capable of producing an output voltage either higher or lower than its input voltage.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's useful when the input voltage might swing both above and below the desired regulated output, such as with a discharging battery.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: The rate at which a power converter's semiconductor switches turn on and off.
terms.simpleExplanation: A higher switching frequency generally allows smaller passive components, at the cost of higher switching losses.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: The fraction of one switching period during which a power converter's switch is turned on.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the primary control variable a power converter adjusts to regulate its output voltage.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electrical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Signals & Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: The output of a linear time-invariant system when its input is an ideal impulse signal.
terms.simpleExplanation: It fully characterizes an LTI system — once known, the system's response to ANY input can be computed via convolution.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Signals & Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A signal defined at every instant of time, taking on a continuous range of values.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the natural representation of physical signals like voltage or sound pressure before they're digitized.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Signals & Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A signal defined only at specific, separated instants in time, typically obtained by sampling a continuous signal.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the form digital signal processing actually operates on, since a computer can't store a truly continuous signal.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Signals & Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: How a system's output amplitude and phase change relative to its input, as a function of input frequency.
terms.simpleExplanation: It shows exactly which frequencies a system passes, amplifies, or attenuates — the basis for designing filters.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Signals & Systems
terms.simpleDefinition: A representation of a periodic signal as a sum of sine and cosine waves at different frequencies.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the theoretical foundation for understanding any periodic signal in terms of its frequency content.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A digital circuit whose output depends only on its current inputs, with no memory of past inputs.
terms.simpleExplanation: Logic gates alone, wired together with no feedback, always form a combinational circuit — like a simple adder or multiplexer.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A digital circuit whose output depends on both its current inputs and its past state, stored in memory elements.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's what gives digital systems memory — every register, counter, and state machine is built from sequential circuits.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A combinational circuit that adds two single binary digits, producing a sum and a carry output.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the simplest building block of binary addition, though it can't account for a carry-in from a previous digit.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A combinational circuit that adds two binary digits plus a carry-in, producing a sum and carry-out.
terms.simpleExplanation: Chaining full adders together is the standard way to build a multi-bit binary adder circuit.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A combinational circuit that converts a binary input code into one active output line out of many.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's used anywhere a binary address needs to select exactly one device or memory location out of several.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A combinational circuit that converts one active input line out of many into a compact binary code.
terms.simpleExplanation: It performs the reverse operation of a decoder, compressing many possible input lines into a compact binary representation.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A combinational circuit that selects one of several input signals and routes it to a single output, based on select lines.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the digital equivalent of a rotary switch, letting one output line carry any of several possible input signals.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A combinational circuit that routes a single input signal to one of several possible outputs, based on select lines.
terms.simpleExplanation: It performs the reverse operation of a multiplexer, distributing one signal to many possible destinations.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A graphical grid-based method for simplifying Boolean expressions by grouping adjacent minterms.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's a quick visual alternative to algebraic Boolean simplification, especially useful for expressions with up to four or five variables.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A basic sequential circuit element that stores a single bit of information, changing state on a clock signal.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the fundamental memory element digital systems are built from — registers and counters are made of many flip-flops working together.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A group of flip-flops used together to store a multi-bit binary value.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the basic storage unit inside a digital processor, holding data or instructions during computation.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A sequential circuit that cycles through a defined sequence of states, typically counting clock pulses.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's used anywhere a digital system needs to track a count, generate timing signals, or divide a clock frequency.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electronic Devices
terms.simpleDefinition: The narrow region around a P-N junction that is depleted of free charge carriers, creating an internal electric field.
terms.simpleExplanation: Its width changes with applied voltage, which is the fundamental mechanism behind how a diode conducts in only one direction.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electronic Devices
terms.simpleDefinition: A voltage applied to a diode in the direction that narrows the depletion region and allows current to flow easily.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the condition under which a diode conducts, letting current pass with only a small voltage drop across it.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electronic Devices
terms.simpleDefinition: A voltage applied to a diode in the direction that widens the depletion region and blocks current flow.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the condition under which a diode blocks current, other than a tiny leakage current, until reverse breakdown occurs.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electronic Devices
terms.simpleDefinition: An amplifier circuit built around a MOSFET, using its gate voltage to control a much larger drain current.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the dominant amplifier building block in modern electronics, valued for its very high input impedance.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Electronic Devices
terms.simpleDefinition: A transistor amplifier configuration providing both voltage and current gain, with the emitter as the common reference terminal.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the most widely used bipolar transistor amplifier configuration because of its strong overall gain.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Analog Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: An op-amp circuit configuration that produces an output signal that is an amplified, phase-inverted version of the input.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's one of the two fundamental op-amp amplifier configurations, offering precise, resistor-set gain.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Analog Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: An op-amp circuit configuration that produces an amplified output signal in phase with the input.
terms.simpleExplanation: Unlike the inverting configuration, it presents a very high input impedance, making it useful for weak signal sources.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Analog Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A filter circuit that allows low-frequency signals through while attenuating higher frequencies.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's used to remove high-frequency noise from a signal, or to smooth out a rectified DC voltage.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Analog Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A filter circuit that allows high-frequency signals through while attenuating lower frequencies.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's commonly used to block unwanted DC offset or low-frequency hum from a signal.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Analog Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: The maximum rate at which an op-amp's output voltage can change, limiting how fast a signal can swing.
terms.simpleExplanation: A slew rate that's too low for a given signal causes distortion, especially for large, fast-changing (high-frequency) signals.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: A signal in its original, unshifted frequency range, before being modulated onto a carrier for transmission.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the raw information signal — modulation shifts it up to a carrier frequency suitable for the actual transmission medium.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: A digital modulation technique that represents binary data by switching a carrier's amplitude between two levels.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the simplest digital modulation scheme, though more susceptible to noise than phase- or frequency-based alternatives.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: A digital modulation technique that represents binary data by switching a carrier between two different frequencies.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's more noise-resistant than amplitude shift keying, which is why it was widely used in early modems.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: A digital modulation technique that represents binary data by changing the phase of a carrier signal.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's more bandwidth-efficient than simpler schemes and forms the basis for many modern high-speed digital communication standards.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Digital Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: The ratio of a signal's power to the power of unwanted background noise, usually expressed in decibels.
terms.simpleExplanation: A higher ratio means a cleaner, more reliably decodable signal — it's one of the most fundamental metrics in all of communications engineering.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Wireless Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: The process of transferring an ongoing call or data session from one cell tower to another as a mobile device moves.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's what lets a phone call continue seamlessly as you drive between the coverage areas of different cell towers.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Wireless Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: The variation in a wireless signal's strength over time or distance, caused by multipath propagation and obstacles.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's why a mobile phone's signal strength can fluctuate even while standing still, as reflected signal paths interfere with each other.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Wireless Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: A wireless transmission technique that spreads a signal over a much wider bandwidth than strictly necessary, improving resistance to interference.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's harder to jam or intercept than a narrowband signal, and is a foundational technology behind many modern wireless standards.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Wireless Communication
terms.simpleDefinition: A family of wireless networking standards that allow devices to connect to a local network without cables, typically over short ranges.
terms.simpleExplanation: It operates on unlicensed radio frequencies and is the dominant technology for wireless internet access indoors.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: VLSI Design
terms.simpleDefinition: A pre-designed, characterized logic block (like a gate or flip-flop) used as a building block in VLSI chip design.
terms.simpleExplanation: Using a library of these pre-verified cells lets chip designers assemble complex circuits far faster than designing every transistor from scratch.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: VLSI Design
terms.simpleDefinition: The physical geometric representation of a circuit's transistors and interconnects as they'll actually be manufactured on a chip.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the final design stage before fabrication, translating a logical circuit design into exact physical patterns on silicon.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: VLSI Design
terms.simpleDefinition: The sequence of chemical and physical steps used to manufacture an integrated circuit on a silicon wafer.
terms.simpleExplanation: The minimum feature size this process can reliably produce is what defines a chip's 'process node,' like 5nm or 7nm.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate electronics & communication engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Fluid Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The study of fluids at rest, and the pressure they exert on their surroundings.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's the branch of fluid mechanics behind concepts like hydraulic presses and why pressure increases with depth in a tank.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate mechanical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Fluid Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The study of fluid motion — velocity and acceleration of fluid particles — without considering the forces causing it.
terms.simpleExplanation: It describes HOW a fluid moves, using concepts like streamlines, before kinetics brings in the forces responsible.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate mechanical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Fluid Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The principle that mass is conserved as a fluid flows through a pipe or channel of varying cross-section.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's why water speeds up when a hose nozzle narrows — the same mass must pass through a smaller area in the same time.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate mechanical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Fluid Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The force a fluid exerts perpendicular to a surface, per unit area.
terms.simpleExplanation: It increases with depth in a static fluid and is the driving force behind fluid flow whenever a pressure difference exists.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate mechanical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Fluid Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: A material's mass per unit volume.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's a key property distinguishing fluids and directly affects buoyancy and the pressure a fluid column exerts.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate mechanical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Fluid Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The upward force a fluid exerts on a submerged or floating object, equal to the weight of fluid displaced.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's why a ship made of steel can float — as long as it displaces enough water to equal its own weight.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate mechanical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Fluid Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: A device that measures fluid flow rate by measuring the pressure drop across a constriction in a pipe.
terms.simpleExplanation: It applies Bernoulli's principle directly — the pressure drop at the narrowed section is a direct, measurable indicator of flow speed.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate mechanical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Fluid Mechanics
terms.simpleDefinition: The thin layer of fluid near a solid surface where viscosity slows the flow relative to the free stream.
terms.simpleExplanation: Its behavior — laminar or turbulent — significantly affects the drag a body experiences moving through a fluid.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate mechanical engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Software Engineering
terms.simpleDefinition: Quantitative measures used to assess a software project's size, complexity, quality, or progress.
terms.simpleExplanation: They give teams objective data — like defect density or code complexity — to track quality instead of relying on gut feeling.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate software engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Software Engineering
terms.simpleDefinition: The probability that software will operate without failure for a specified period under specified conditions.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's measured and improved through testing, and is especially critical for safety-related or high-availability systems.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate software engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Software Engineering
terms.simpleDefinition: Restructuring existing code to improve its internal structure without changing its external behavior.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's how a codebase is kept maintainable over time, paying down technical debt without adding new features.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate software engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Software Engineering
terms.simpleDefinition: An older software system still in active use, often built with outdated technology but still critical to operations.
terms.simpleExplanation: Maintaining or replacing one is a major real-world software engineering challenge, since it often lacks documentation and modern tooling.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate software engineering curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: A power electronic system that controls the speed and torque of an electric motor by converting and regulating its supply power.
terms.simpleExplanation: It's one of the most common real-world applications of power electronics, used in everything from industrial pumps to electric vehicles.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate power electronics curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: Circuit techniques used to make an electrical load draw current more in phase with its voltage, improving power factor.
terms.simpleExplanation: It reduces wasted reactive power and the associated losses and equipment oversizing that a poor power factor causes.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate power electronics curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: Unwanted distortion of an AC waveform caused by frequency components that are multiples of the fundamental frequency.
terms.simpleExplanation: Power electronic switching converters are a major source of it, and excessive harmonics can damage equipment and waste energy.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate power electronics curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).

terms.subject: Power Electronics
terms.simpleDefinition: Unwanted electrical noise generated by fast-switching circuits that can disrupt the operation of nearby electronic equipment.
terms.simpleExplanation: Power converters' rapid switching is a major source of it, which is why they're designed with filtering and shielding to limit it.
terms.source: Standard undergraduate power electronics curriculum (common across AICTE-aligned Indian universities).
